The core mathematical structure of WSNs emerges from the interplay between node-level constraints and network-level coordination. Each sensor node is modeled as a discrete entity with bounded energy E_node, processing C_proc, and storage S_mem, forming a constraint tuple. These nodes form a graph G(V,E) where V represents nodes and E represents communication links. Multi-hop routing is a path-finding problem in this graph, minimizing cost functions such as energy expenditure or hop count. The network's reliability depends on the robustness of this graph under node failures, modeled as stochastic events. The aggregation principle implies that the global behavior of the network can be described by a sum or integral of local functions f_i(x_i), where x_i is the sensory input at node i. This leads to a derived kernel in GSE that computes global observables from local measurements. The failure modes include energy exhaustion, link disconnection, and node malfunction, each leading to breakdown regimes in either routing or aggregation. The mathematical duality lies in the trade-off between localized autonomy and global coherence, which is encoded in the routing protocol's optimization criteria.
